chunks: Muhammad ibn Hammam and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Jumhoor all narrated, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Jumhoor, from his father, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Salih ibn Maytham and Yahya ibn Sabiq all, from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir (peace be upon him) that he said:
The hasteners perished, and those nearest [to Allah] were saved, and the fortress remained firm on its pegs. Indeed, after distress there is a wonderful deliverance.

key_terms.أَصْحَابُ الْمَحَاضِيرِ: The hasteners; those who rushed to claim imamate/leadership before their time
key_terms.الْحِصْنُ: The fortress; metaphor for the stable authority or Imamate
key_terms.الْغَمِّ: Distress or grief; referring to the period of waiting or hardship
key_terms.الْمُقَرَّبُونَ: The those nearest; referring to the Imams who are close to Allah
key_terms.فَتْحًا عَجِيبًا: A wonderful deliverance or opening; a significant victory after hardship

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'hasteners' and 'those nearest' in the context of waiting for deliverance?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kitab al-Ghayba* addresses the core Shia doctrine of *al-intizar* (waiting for the Reappearance), distinguishing between the 'hasteners' (*al-muhadirin*) who prematurely claimed authority and the 'nearest' (*al-muqarrabun*) who remained steadfast. The metaphor of the fortress anchored by its pegs underscores the enduring stability of the Imamate against transient political claims, while the promise of 'wonderful opening' after 'grief' provides theological comfort during the period of occultation.
